content.title: Is the gold bull still alive? Analysts say that during the previous two bull markets, there were multiple significant pullbacks, and declines presented good opportunities to increase positions.
content.text: Analysts pointed out that although gold prices experienced a historic single-day plunge last week, this is merely a typical technical correction within a long-term bull market. All major gold bull markets since 1971 have undergone multiple significant corrections, and the current decline instead offers investors a rare opportunity to increase their holdings. The core rationale supporting the long-term strengthening of gold—geopolitical uncertainties, continued central bank gold purchases, and expectations of a weakening US dollar—remains unchanged.Despite experiencing a historic plunge last week, market observers believe that the bull market in gold is far from over. Analysts generally view the recent sharp volatility as a temporary correction within a long-term uptrend rather than a structural reversal. Historical data suggests that such corrections often present opportunities to re-enter the market.The precious metals market has recently experienced significant turbulence. After surging 66% throughout 2025 and continuing into early 2026, gold prices plummeted nearly 10% in a single day last Friday, dragging down silver, palladium, and platinum significantly. The trigger for this sell-off was the nomination of Wash as the next Federal Reserve Chair, which the market interpreted as easing prior concerns about the Fed's independence. This marked the most severe single-day decline for gold in 13 years.However, the market quickly entered a recovery mode. As investors reassessed the situation, $XAU/USD (XAUUSD.CFD)$ a strong rebound of over 6% occurred on Tuesday, closing near $4,946.81 per ounce. The upward momentum continued into Wednesday, with gold surpassing $5,000 as of this writing.Institutional strategists noted that despite signals flashing 'overvalued' on screens, the geopolitical tensions, trade policy uncertainties, and debt-related concerns supporting gold prices have not dissipated. Analysis from multiple investment banks indicates that the current downturn has not undermined the long-term investment rationale but may instead represent a buying opportunity within this historic bull market.History Repeats: Normality of Corrections in Bull MarketsRuss Mould, Investment Director at AJ Bell, highlighted in a Monday report that gold is currently in its third major bull market since 1971, with both previous bull markets experiencing multiple significant corrections.Mould analyzed that the bull market from 1971 to 1980 began when President Nixon severed the link between the dollar and gold, followed by a surge in U.S. deficits, oil shocks, and soaring inflation, driving gold prices from $35 per ounce to a peak of $835 in 1980. According to data from AJ Bell and LSEG, gold prices fell multiple times during this period, with the longest 'correction phase' lasting 105 days and the sharpest decline reaching 19.4%.Similarly, during the bull market from 2001 to 2011, records show five price corrections, each with declines up to 16%. Mould noted that the current bull market began in 2015 and had already experienced five corrections before last Friday's pullback, including a drop of over 20% in 2022. He emphasized that geopolitical uncertainty, stubborn inflation, and skyrocketing government debt form the foundation of gold investment. "Since these issues remain unchanged compared to last week, this sudden decline might be an opportunity to increase holdings."Central Bank Demand and Valuation PremiumGeorge Cheveley, Portfolio Manager of the Natural Resources team at Ninety One Global Investment Management, told CNBC that the current strength of gold aligns more with a late-cycle environment rather than the early stages of a speculative rebound from a historical perspective. However, he added that a key differentiating factor in this cycle is the scale and persistence of central bank demand.Cheveley noted in an email that central bank demand has become a more significant market driver than ever before, providing structural support that was historically absent during the same period. Although data from the World Gold Council shows that net gold purchases by central banks fell to 328 tons in 2025 from 345 tons the previous year, Cheveley believes that as long as real yields remain low and uncertainties surrounding growth, debt, and geopolitics persist, gold will maintain its resilience.Strategists at Barclays also stated in a report on Tuesday that although models indicate gold is 'overvalued' relative to a fair value of approximately $4,000, this premium appears sustainable and does not signify a bubble. They pointed out that historical cycles show that misalignments between price and fair value can last for years, with inflation, U.S. policy issues, and the long-term depreciation trend of the dollar supporting elevated gold prices.The loss of Federal Reserve credibility is not the only signal of an end.The Chief Investment Office of UBS Group noted in a report titled 'Not the End' on Monday that gold bull markets do not typically conclude merely due to the dissipation of fear or excessively high prices; they only end when central banks restore credibility and shift to a new monetary policy framework.UBS analysis indicates that the stringent monetary policies implemented by Paul Volcker in 1980 effectively restored the credibility of the Federal Reserve, leading to a significant rise in real interest rates and a prolonged appreciation of the dollar, which ended the gold bull market at that time. However, UBS strategists believe that since Kevin Warsh has not yet demonstrated credibility equivalent to Volcker's, the current sell-off does not mark the end of the bull market. Over the past year, the U.S. Dollar Index has fallen by more than 10%, reflecting concerns about central bank independence and the White House's policy mix.The UBS team believes that gold is currently in the middle-to-late stages of this bull market, transitioning from a sustained upward trajectory to a phase characterized by new highs but accompanied by intermittent pullbacks of 5-8%. The report emphasizes that typical factors ending a gold bull market—persistently high real interest rates, a structurally stronger dollar, improved geopolitics, and fully restored central bank credibility—are currently absent. UBS predicts that gold prices will reach $6,200 next month before retreating to $5,900 by the end of the year.Editor/Doris
